title: Routing Fundamentals
summary: What routing is, how to read a routing table, connected and local routes, and how routers pick the most specific matching route.

content.body:
**Routing** is the process routers use to determine the path that IP packets should take across a network to reach their destination.

Switches forward frames using a **MAC address table**; routers forward packets using a **routing table**, which holds all of the router's known destination **networks**. When a router receives a packet, it looks in the routing table for the best route to forward it.

A **route** is an instruction to the router: *"to send a packet to destination X, send it to next-hop Y"* — where a **next-hop** is the next router in the path. If the destination is directly connected, send it straight to the destination; if it's the router's own address, receive it for itself.

There are two main ways routers learn routes:

- **Dynamic routing** — routers share routes automatically using protocols like OSPF.
- **Static routing** — an engineer manually configures routes.

This lesson covers two route types that are neither: **connected** and **local** routes.

steps.narration: Four routers form a WAN (wide area network). R1 and R4 each connect a LAN (192.168.1.0/24 for PC1, 192.168.4.0/24 for PC4). The router-to-router links are the WAN networks.
R2–R4 is 192.168.24.0/24 (R2 .2, R4 .4); R3–R4 is 192.168.34.0/24 (R3 .3, R4 .4). Notice each router's address matches its number (R1 = .1, R2 = .2, …).

content.body:
When you configure an IP address on an interface and enable it with `no shutdown`, **two routes are added automatically** — one connected and one local.

A **connected route** is a route to the *network* the interface is connected to, shown with code **C** in `show ip route`. If R1's G0/2 is `192.168.1.1/24`, the connected route is to `192.168.1.0/24`.

It tells the router: *"to send a packet to any host in this network, send it out of that interface"* — matching every address from `192.168.1.0` to `192.168.1.255`.

A **local route** is a route to the *exact* IP address configured on the interface, shown with code **L**. It uses a **/32** mask, meaning all 32 bits are fixed — it matches only that single address (e.g. `192.168.1.1/32`).

It tells the router: *"packets to this destination are for me — receive them, don't forward them."*

Because `/32` has all netmask bits set to 1 (255.255.255.255), only the one address matches. This contrasts with `/24`, where only the first 24 bits are fixed.

`show ip route` output has two parts:

- **Codes legend** — maps the route code letters to how the route was learned (`L` = local, `C` = connected, `S` = static, `O` = OSPF, …).
- **Routes** — the actual route entries.

A connected route appears as:

```
C   192.168.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
```

A local route appears as:

```
L   192.168.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
```

So an interface with an IP address produces **two** routes: `C` for the network and `L` for the address. R1, with three configured interfaces, has six routes. (Ignore the `variably subnetted` summary lines — they're not routes.)

A route **matches** a packet's destination if that destination IP falls within the network the route describes. A packet to `192.168.1.60` matches `192.168.1.0/24`, but not `192.168.2.0/24`.

When several routes match, the router uses the **most specific** match — the one with the **longest prefix length**. A packet to `192.168.1.1` matches both `192.168.1.0/24` and `192.168.1.1/32`; the `/32` local route wins, so R1 receives the packet for itself.

Two key differences from switches:

- **Switches flood** unknown-destination frames; **routers never flood** — they **drop** packets with no matching route.
- Switches look for an **exact match** in the MAC table; routers look for the **most specific match**.

content.body: Remember the pair: configuring an IP address + `no shutdown` adds a **Connected** route (to the network) and a **Local** route (to the interface's own address). And the router-forwarding rules: **never flood**; **drop** if no route matches; pick the **most specific (longest-prefix)** route when several match.

questions.question: The IP address configured on a router interface will appear in the routing table as what kind of route?
questions.explanation: Configuring an IP address (and enabling the interface) adds two routes: a connected route (to the network) and a local route (to the exact IP address). The interface's own IP address appears as a local route.

questions.question: R1 has a local route to 192.168.3.25/32. What will R1 do when it receives a packet destined for 192.168.3.25?
questions.explanation: A local /32 route means that address is configured on one of R1's own interfaces. Packets to it are for R1 itself, so R1 receives the packet rather than forwarding it.

questions.question: How does a router behave when it receives a packet for which it has no matching route?
questions.explanation: Unlike switches, which flood frames with unknown destinations (unknown unicast), routers never flood. If no route matches, the router drops the packet.

options.label: A
options.text: It floods the packet out all interfaces

options.label: C
options.text: It sends it to the default gateway

questions.question: Which two types of routes are automatically added to the routing table when you configure an IP address on an interface and enable it?
questions.explanation: In `show ip route`, C stands for Connected and L for Local. Both are added automatically when you configure an IP address on an interface and bring it up with `no shutdown`.

questions.question: R1's routing table has routes to 10.0.1.0/24 and 10.0.1.23/32. It receives a packet destined for 10.0.1.23. How many routes match, and which is selected?
questions.explanation: Both routes match destination 10.0.1.23. The most specific matching route is the /32 local route to 10.0.1.23, so that route is selected — R1 receives the packet for itself.

options.label: C
options.text: Two matches; the /32 route is most specific

options.label: D
options.text: No match; the packet is dropped
